summaries.week-2-section: Stanford Research Park is the first university-owned industrial park, created by leasing land that the university was barred from selling.

week-2-section.text: Fred Terman created the Stanford Research Park (1951) by leasing land the university could not sell.
The Research Park fostered a working loop where companies recruited students and funded research from the university.
Fred Terman promoted an applied-engineering culture at Stanford to serve the military-industrial complex.

links.title: Silicon Valley Pioneers
links.reason: Fred Terman is a key figure associated with the creation of Stanford Research Park.

summaries.week-2-section: Venture capital is a form of investment that finances high-risk startups by taking equity and absorbing potential losses, which was initially supported by government programs.

week-2-section.text: Georges Doriot is cited as the first venture capitalist, operating ARDC (1946) and funding DEC.
The federal SBIC program (1958) leveraged private risk capital by lending government money for every dollar of private capital.
Venture capital has become an insular 'old-boys network' where insider connections dictate deal flow.

links.title: Origins of Silicon Valley
links.reason: Venture Capital is a form of investment that helped finance the high-risk startups central to the emergence of Silicon Valley.

summaries.week-2-section: The counterculture ethos of the 1960s merged with technology, leading to a philosophy of personal liberation through computing.

week-2-section.text: The Berkeley Free Speech Movement (1964) was part of the Bay Area's counterculture, which distrusted big institutions.
Lee Felsenstein and Pam Hardt-English created Community Memory, a public computer terminal in a Berkeley record store.
The anti-establishment ethos became the self-image of the industry, surviving even as companies became large corporations.

links.title: Origins of Silicon Valley
links.reason: The counterculture ethos of the 1960s merged with technology, contributing to the ethos of the industry during Silicon Valley's emergence.

summaries.week-2-section: California's legal framework supports tech innovation by allowing firms to take equity and by prohibiting non-compete agreements.

week-2-section.text: Valley law firms built the scaffolding for startups by taking equity instead of fees, similar to venture capital.
California's refusal to enforce non-competes allows engineers to job-hop, promoting the cross-pollination of ideas.
The same law firms may draft term sheets for investors and the startup, creating an inherent conflict of interest.

links.title: Venture Capital
links.reason: The legal system's practice of valley law firms taking equity instead of fees is similar to the model used by venture capital.

summaries.week-3-section: The Team Start-Up Competition requires students to adopt a real early-stage startup, interview its founder, and pitch it at Demo Day, accounting for 20% of the course grade.

week-3-section.text: The competition is worth 20% of the course grade, plus 5% for the founder interview.
The competition arc includes picking a startup, submitting a Start-Up Proposal due 10/11, and presenting the founder interview on 10/27–10/30.
Teams must choose four roles: Team Lead, Industry Lead, Finance Lead, and Marketing & Tech Lead.
Demo Days are scheduled for 11/13, 11/17, 11/19, and 11/20, with the Final Competition on 12/1.

links.title: Founder Interview
links.reason: The Team Start-Up Competition requires students to conduct a founder interview as part of its requirements.

links.title: Startup Selection Rules
links.reason: The Team Start-Up Competition requires students to adopt a real early-stage startup, which is governed by selection rules.

summaries.week-3-section: Startups must meet specific criteria to be eligible for the competition, including being pre-Series A, founded in Silicon Valley, and no more than three years old.

week-3-section.text: A startup must be pre–Series A, founded in Silicon Valley (SF / East Bay), no more than 3 years old, and have only seed funding.
Startups can be found through Y Combinator, Berkeley SkyDeck, or a16z Speedrun.
Teams must claim their chosen startup in the shared Google Sheet on a first-come, first-served basis.

links.title: Team Start-Up Competition
links.reason: Startup Selection Rules define the criteria for eligibility in the Team Start-Up Competition.

summaries.week-3-section: Several online platforms are provided to help students research and verify the details of potential startups.

week-3-section.text: Y Combinator directory can be filtered by Status = Active, Batch = recent, Industry, and Location = SF Bay Area.
Berkeley SkyDeck portfolio lists Berkeley-affiliated founders, referencing current Batch and Pad-13 cohorts.
Pitchbook is a database used to confirm a startup's stage, age, and HQ, with limits of ≤ 10 rows/day and ≤ 25 rows/month for UCB students.

summaries.week-5-section: Building a professional profile involves gaining experience through various activities that provide evidence and connections.

week-5-section.text: Middle steps to build a profile include earning a certification, joining a club, entering a competition, and doing pro bono work.
Each profile-building activity provides evidence, a story, and people who can vouch for the individual.

links.reason: Entering a competition is listed as a middle step to build a professional profile.

summaries.week-2-section: Several individuals were instrumental in shaping the technological and institutional foundations of Silicon Valley.

week-2-section.text: Vannevar Bush ran WWII federal R&D and advocated for permanent federal science funding with 'Science, the Endless Frontier' (1945).
Fred Terman is known as the 'Father of Silicon Valley' for bringing the MIT military/industry model to Stanford.
William Shockley co-invented the transistor in 1956, leading to Shockley Semiconductor (1956).
Arthur Rock financed the 'Traitorous Eight' and made 'venture capitalist' a job title by funding and chairing Intel.

links.title: Stanford Research Park
links.reason: Fred Terman brought the MIT military/industry model to Stanford, which led to the creation of Stanford Research Park.

links.title: Venture Capital
links.reason: Arthur Rock made 'venture capitalist' a job title by funding and chairing Intel.

summaries.week-2-section: The five pillars are the foundational elements that have shaped and maintained Silicon Valley's competitive edge over the long term.

week-2-section.text: The state / government policy War and great-power competition have driven US innovation for 80 years.
Research universities supply the people, with Stanford noted for its applied-engineering culture and Research Park.
Venture capital provides funding for ventures that banks would not touch, often taking equity.
Immigrants constitute a significant portion of high-tech firms and Bay Area residents.
The legal system in California supports innovation by refusing to enforce non-competes.

summaries.week-2-section: Silicon Valley emerged from an agricultural area, evolving into a federally funded research and defense economy driven by wartime and Cold War investment.

week-2-section.text: Before the war, the area was known as the “Valley of Heart's Delight” and featured a small radio-and-electronics cluster.
World War II saw Vannevar Bush's Office of Scientific Research and Development pour federal money into university labs.
Sputnik (1957) triggered a surge in funding through NASA, ARPA, and the National Defense Education Act (1958).
The ecosystem led to the spin-out of semiconductors: Shockley (1956) $\rightarrow$ Fairchild (1957) $\rightarrow$ Intel (1968).

links.title: Stanford Research Park
links.reason: Silicon Valley Emergence is directly related to Stanford Research Park as the latter is a physical manifestation of the research ecosystem that emerged.

summaries.week-3-section: The founder interview is a graded checkpoint where the entire team must participate in a 30–60 minute discussion with the startup's founder or a tech professional.

week-3-section.text: The interview should be 30–60 minutes long, conducted on Zoom or in person, with every team member present.
The deliverable requires 3 slides and a 5–7 minute presentation with equal speaking time.
Teams should prepare 4–5 core questions, with one person moderating and one taking notes.

summaries.week-3-section: Students are advised to begin outreach immediately due to the time founders take to respond, and they should use professional methods to contact founders.

week-3-section.text: Founders can take 2–3 weeks to reply, so teams should line up a backup person early.
Methods for reaching founders include SkyDeck company pages, LinkedIn, and the YC company page.
Emails must be professional, stating who the student is, the class, why they chose the company, and proposing two specific times for a 30–45 minute Zoom call.

week-2-section.text: About 25% of US high-tech firms had an immigrant founder; about 40% of Valley firms by the internet era.

week-5-section.text: Immigrants have for decades come to Silicon Valley for education and become company founders.
